volumes.title: The Key and the Notebook
volumes.text:
January. The garden at Number Nine, Tanner's Row came to me with a rusty key, a wheelbarrow with a flat tyre, and my great-uncle Corwin's notebook. Thirty years I sold ferry tickets at Ember Quay. I know tides and timetables. I do not know gardens.

The notebook's first page carries one rule, underlined twice: Wait a full year before you dig up anything you cannot name. Below it, in smaller writing: This will be harder than it sounds.

So today I only walked the paths. Everything is brown and flattened. By the south wall stands a bare grey stick, tall as my shoulder, with no label and no sign of life. My new neighbour, Mr. Hask, looked over the wall and said it had been dead for years. I cannot name it. By the rule, it stays.

volumes.title: Snowdrops Under the Hedge
volumes.text:
February. I came out this morning meaning to rake the dead leaves from under the hawthorn hedge, because a tidy garden seemed the least I could manage. Uncle Corwin's notebook stopped me. His February page says only: Leave the leaves. Look under the hedge on a mild day.

I looked. Snowdrops, hundreds of them, pushing up through the brown litter like small white lanterns. I would have dragged a rake straight across their necks.

So I fetched a kneeling mat instead and counted, as I used to count passengers on the Ember ferry. I gave up at two hundred and forty. Mr. Hask, next door, says his own snowdrops are finished already, and looked a little put out. The grey stick by the south wall has done nothing whatever. I checked it twice, which I suspect is once more than a patient person would.

volumes.title: Sweet Peas on the Sill
volumes.text:
March. At last the notebook lets me do something. Sow sweet peas indoors, it says, one to a pot, and then go away. I filled twelve pots on the kitchen table at Number Nine, pushed a seed into each to the depth of my first knuckle, and lined them along the sill.

That was nine days ago. I have looked at them, by my own reckoning, some sixty times. Nothing. A ferry at least keeps to a timetable.

Mr. Hask leaned over the wall while I was sweeping the path and nodded at the grey stick. “You'll want that out before spring,” he said. “I've a good spade.” I thanked him and said it was not yet a year. This morning, the tenth day, one pot showed a pale green hook pushing up the soil. I told nobody. I simply stood there while the kettle went cold.

volumes.title: The Weeds That Weren't
volumes.text:
April. The gravel path was thick with seedlings, grey-green and hairy, and I had the hoe in my hand. Uncle Corwin's rule held me back: nothing dug up that I cannot name. I could not name these. I put the hoe away with poor grace and weeded the things I did know, which were dandelions and more dandelions.

This week the seedlings opened. Forget-me-nots, a blue river of them running the whole length of the path to the gate on Tanner's Row. People have stopped to look. The baker's girl asked if I had planned it.

I said the garden had planned it and I had merely kept out of the way, which is the most honest sentence I have spoken about gardening so far. The sweet peas are out against the fence, eight of the twelve. The stick by the south wall is still a stick.

volumes.title: Too Soon for Beans
volumes.text:
May. I have learned what impatience costs, and it costs fourteen runner beans. The first week of the month was warm as a bakehouse, so I planted them out along their poles, a fortnight ahead of the date in Uncle Corwin's notebook. I thought the notebook was being fussy.

On the ninth night a frost came down off the Northern Fells. By morning every bean hung black and limp. Mr. Hask, whose own beans were still safe on his windowsill, had the kindness to say nothing at all, which was worse.

I have sown fourteen more. They sit indoors at Number Nine until the date written down, and not an hour before. One good thing came of my sulking round the garden: the grey stick by the south wall has buds on it. Small, tight, green ones. So it is alive. I still cannot name it.

volumes.title: Peonies and Plain Leaves
volumes.text:
June. The bed beside the water butt looked so empty in winter that I nearly gave it over to cabbages. Now it holds eleven peonies, each bloom the size of a soup plate and the pink of the inside of a shell. Uncle Corwin's notebook says they sulked four years before flowering, and that he moved them once and was punished with three more.

I cut one for the kitchen table at Number Nine and felt like a thief.

The stick by the south wall has come into leaf. I had hoped for something grand. The leaves are long, plain and rather rough, the sort you would not look at twice in a hedge. Mr. Hask examined them over the wall and pronounced it a weed with ideas above its station. He may be right. But I waited for the forget-me-nots, and I can wait for a weed.

volumes.title: The Work of Sitting Still
volumes.text:
July. No rain for three weeks. Every evening I carry twenty cans from the water butt, ten to the beans and ten to the sweet peas, and my arms have opinions about it. The notebook's advice for the month is brief: Water the roots, not the leaves. Then sit on the bench. Sitting is part of the work.

I did not believe that last part. I am a person who ticked off ferry sailings for thirty years. But I tried it, with a cup of tea, at the hour when the swifts come screaming down Tanner's Row.

From the bench I saw things I had walked past all summer. A blackbird has a path of its own under the currants. The sweet peas want tying in. And the plain-leaved shrub by the south wall, which I no longer call a stick, has grown a full hand's width since June.

volumes.title: A Glut of Beans
volumes.text:
August. The second sowing of runner beans, the one I made after the May frost took the first, has repaid me beyond all reason. I picked four pounds on Monday and four more on Thursday, and they are hanging there again today, long as rulers.

I have eaten beans buttered, beans in soup and beans cold with vinegar. I have left bags of them on doorsteps along Tanner's Row like a burglar working backwards. Mr. Hask accepted his with dignity and returned the bag an hour later full of plums.

Uncle Corwin's notebook says to leave the six fattest pods on the plant until they rattle, then shell them and keep the seed dry for spring. So some of this summer is to be put away in a jam jar. I find I like that. A year ago I did not own a single thing that needed waiting for.

volumes.title: Eleven Apples
volumes.text:
September. There is an old apple tree in the corner by the shed, bent like a man looking for a dropped coin. Mr. Hask told me it had not fruited in his time. I had it marked in my mind for firewood, once my year of waiting was up.

On Saturday I went to prop the shed door and found eleven apples in the top of the tree, small, striped and red. I got them down with a walking stick and a colander.

They are sharp enough to make the eyes water, and in a pie they are the best I ever tasted. Uncle Corwin's notebook calls the tree Old Crooked and says it bears every second year, when it chooses. I took a slice round to Mr. Hask. He ate it standing at the wall and asked, quite humbly, for the name of the apple.

volumes.title: Leaves and a Paper Bag
volumes.text:
October. The garden at Number Nine is coming apart gently, like a parcel being unwrapped. I rake the leaves into a wire pen behind the shed, where Uncle Corwin's notebook says they will turn to good black leaf mould in two years. Two years! In January I would have laughed. Now I only wrote the date on a slate and propped it against the wire.

A paper bag came from the seedsman in Emberwick: fifty daffodils and thirty tulips, looking like so many small onions.

I planted them on my knees all Tuesday afternoon, each one in the dark with its nose up, and when I had finished there was nothing whatever to see. It is the strangest work I know, burying things on trust. The shrub by the south wall is turning yellow. Its leaves are dropping one by one, and it has still told me nothing.

volumes.title: Mr. Hask's Good Spade
volumes.text:
November. The shrub by the south wall is a bare grey stick again, exactly as I found it in January. Ten months of looking, and all it gave me was a summer of plain leaves. Mr. Hask came round with his good spade over his shoulder. “Nearly your year,” he said. “Shall I?”

I will be truthful: I almost said yes. The spot would suit a rose.

Instead I asked him in out of the wind and went through Uncle Corwin's notebook once more, page by page. Tucked in the back cover was a seedsman's receipt, seven years old, and on it in his writing: Wintersweet, for the south wall. Flowers on bare wood in the dark of the year. They say seven winters before the first. Do not let anyone talk you out of it. Mr. Hask read it twice and carried his spade home.

volumes.title: Wintersweet at Last
volumes.text:
December. I went out to the south wall this morning in my coat and slippers, with frost on every path at Number Nine, and smelled it before I saw it. Something like honey and spice, in a month when nothing has any business smelling of anything.

The grey stick is in flower. Small waxy bells, pale yellow with a stain of dark red inside, strung all along the bare wood. Uncle Corwin planted it seven winters ago and never saw this. I stood there until my feet went numb, and then I fetched Mr. Hask, who took his hat off.

Tonight there is a sprig in a jug on the kitchen table and the whole house is sweet with it. I have opened the notebook to the first clean page and written my own line under his rule, for whoever comes after me: He was right. Wait.

volumes.title: A Mile of Hedge
volumes.text:
January. These are the notes of Wilf Tarrant, hedger to the parish of Emberwick, kept for one year on the Long Hedge. It runs a mile along the Lowlands road, from the last house in town to Sallow Gate, and it has been let go for twenty years. It is tall, thin at the bottom and full of holes a sheep could stroll through.

The parish has given me the winter to lay it, and a boy to help. Pim Oakes is twelve and has never held a billhook. Today I showed him the cut: three parts through the stem, low and slanting, so the stem bends over but still lives. We call the laid stem a pleacher.

He watched, and said it seemed unkind to the tree. I told him to come back and look in May. We laid forty yards before the light went.

volumes.title: Forty Whips
volumes.text:
February. Halfway along the Long Hedge, by the stile, there is a gap eleven paces wide where the old thorns died out and nothing but nettle grows. You cannot lay what is not there. So the parish sent to the nursery at Emberwick for forty whips, and Pim Oakes and I planted them today in a double row.

A whip is a young tree no thicker than a pencil and about as impressive. We put in twenty-four hawthorn, eight hazel, four field maple and four dog rose, each one heeled in firm with a boot.

Pim wanted to know how long before they made a hedge. I said seven years to be useful and fifteen to be handsome. He worked out aloud that he would be twenty-seven. I said I would be eighty-one, and that we had better both keep an eye on them.

volumes.title: Blackthorn Winter
volumes.text:
March. The blackthorn is out along the Long Hedge, white blossom on black wood before a single leaf has shown. From the Emberwick end it looks as though somebody has thrown a bedsheet over the far half-mile. With it comes the cold snap the old people call the blackthorn winter. It comes every year, and every year the town is surprised.

Pim Oakes and I laid the last stretch to Sallow Gate with numb fingers, and drove the final stake on the nineteenth. One mile, laid, staked and bound along the top with hazel rods.

It looks raw. The cuts show pale and the whole line leans one way like grass after wind. Pim stood back and said nothing, which is his way of saying it looks a ruin. We put the billhooks away oiled. From now until autumn the hedge belongs to the birds.

volumes.title: Nests, and Hands Off
volumes.text:
April. No hedger cuts in April. The rule is older than the parish of Emberwick, and the reason for it is sitting on five eggs. So Pim Oakes and I walk the Long Hedge with our hands in our pockets and a notebook, and call it work.

We have found nine nests in the mile. Two blackbirds, a song thrush, three dunnocks, a pair of long-tailed tits with a ball of moss and cobweb like a knitted purse, and two wrens. One wren has built inside the pleachers we laid in January, a yard from the road, bold as a toll-keeper.

Pim found that one himself and has told nobody but me. Every laid stem is breaking into leaf along its length, just as I promised him. He admits now that the cut was not unkind. Of the forty whips by the stile, thirty-nine show green. One hawthorn never woke.

volumes.title: May Blossom
volumes.text:
May. The hawthorn has flowered, and the Long Hedge is white from the last house in Emberwick to Sallow Gate. The scent is heavy, sweet, and not quite pleasant up close, which never stops anyone from burying a nose in it. Carters slow their horses to look. The stems Pim Oakes and I laid in winter are flowering as freely as the uncut ones, lying on their sides.

Under the hedge the bank has come up in stitchwort, red campion and the frothy white stuff children call lady's lace. Pim has started a list of flowers on the back page of my notebook. He is at twenty-two and spells most of them his own way.

Bad news by the stile. A rabbit has bitten two of the hazel whips clean through. Thirty-seven left of the forty, all in leaf. We fenced the gap with wire netting, a month late.

volumes.title: Roses in the Dry
volumes.text:
June. Dog rose and honeysuckle have taken over from the hawthorn. The roses are pale pink, flat as saucers and gone in two days; the honeysuckle smells strongest at dusk, when the big moths come to it. Walking the Long Hedge home to Emberwick in the evening is the best part of my wage.

But there has been no rain for a month, and the new whips by the stile are feeling it. Their leaves hang like wet washing. Old hedge has roots down to the cool; a whip planted in February has roots about the length of my hand.

So Pim Oakes and I carry water from the Sallow Gate trough, two buckets each on a yoke, three hundred paces there and three hundred back. Pim has given several of the whips names, which I advised against. It only makes the counting harder when one goes.

volumes.title: Who Lives Here
volumes.text:
July. Rain at last, two whole days of it, and the Long Hedge drank it standing. It came too late for two of the hawthorn whips by the stile, which had gone brown and brittle. Thirty-five of the forty remain. Pim Oakes took it hard. One of the two was called Gerald.

To cheer him I set him a census: every creature seen in or under the hedge in one week. He has filled four pages. A hedgehog that crosses the road at the same spot each dusk. Bank voles. A slow-worm under a flat stone. Yellowhammers, whitethroats, and the wren's second brood in the pleachers. Eleven sorts of butterfly, of which he could name seven.

He asked me how many lived in the mile altogether. I said nobody had ever finished counting, and that a hedge is a town with one long, thin street. He wrote that down too.

volumes.title: Harvest Carts
volumes.text:
August. The corn is coming in off the Lowlands, and the wagons go by the Long Hedge so heaped that the hawthorn combs straw off the top of every load. By evening the whole mile wears a yellow fringe, and the sparrows of Emberwick come out to pick it over.

The hedge has turned from flower to fruit. Haws are still green, sloes hard and dusty blue, hazelnuts pale in their frilled cups. The first blackberries are ripe at the sunny end by the town. Pim Oakes eats them faster than he picks and arrives each morning with a purple chin.

We mend the stile and scythe the nettles from around the whips. Thirty-five still, and the best hazel has put on a foot of growth. The wren in the pleachers has gone quiet. Her young are out somewhere along the street she built on.

volumes.title: Blackberry Sunday
volumes.text:
September. By old custom the second Sunday of the month is Blackberry Sunday, and half of Emberwick walks out along the Long Hedge with baskets, jugs, basins and one hat-box. I counted sixty people in the mile. The lower berries were stripped by noon; after that it was walking sticks to hook the high sprays down, and small children lifted on shoulders.

Several stopped to look at the laying and said the hedge seemed thicker. It is: every pleacher has thrown up a row of new shoots, straight as candles, and you cannot see through it anywhere now. Pim Oakes explained the cut to the baker at some length. I let him.

His mother sent me a jar of bramble jelly, still warm. The label says Long Hedge in Pim's spelling. The sloes are ripening, and the fieldfares will be here soon for the haws.

volumes.title: The Reckoning by the Stile
volumes.text:
October. Hazelnuts are down, and so are the squirrels, the jays and Pim Oakes, all after the same nuts. The spindle bushes near Sallow Gate have opened their pink berries to show the orange seed, a combination no sensible person would choose and which looks splendid. Spiders have slung webs across every gap in the Long Hedge.

Today we made the autumn count of the whips we planted by the stile in February. Forty went in. Frost, rabbits and the June drought took seven. Thirty-three stand, and the tallest hazel is up to Pim's belt.

Pim thought thirty-three a poor score. I told him it was a good one, and that a hedger who expects forty out of forty should take up carpentry. Next month we plant seven more in the spaces. A hedge is never planted once. It is planted, and then kept.

volumes.title: Pim's First Pleacher
volumes.text:
November. The leaves have come off the Long Hedge, and the work Pim Oakes and I did last winter stands plain: a mile of stems lying slantwise, stakes upright, the hazel binding running along the top like the rim of a basket. It looks like a thing made on purpose. In January it looked like an accident.

The parish has given us the next stretch, the far side of Sallow Gate. I handed Pim the billhook and stood back with my hands behind me, which was the hard part.

He took nine cuts where I would take three. He went too deep on one stem and it snapped, and he looked at me as if he had broken a window. But the next stem bent over sweetly and lay down on its neighbour, alive. We planted the seven new whips before dinner. He counted them in himself.

volumes.title: Fieldfares on the Haws
volumes.text:
December. Hard frost on the Lowlands road, and every twig of the Long Hedge furred white. The fieldfares have come down from the north in their hundreds. They work along the mile from the Emberwick end to Sallow Gate, stripping the haws and chattering like a drawer of spoons. What they drop, the mice have.

So ends my year of notes. One mile laid. Nine nests that I know of. Forty whips planted, thirty-three kept, seven more put in. One apprentice, who can now lay a stem in four cuts and has stopped apologising to the tree.

I am sixty-seven next month, and my shoulder tells me about it. Today I gave Pim Oakes my second billhook, the light one, with his initials burnt into the handle. He will see those whips made into a hedge. I have asked him to keep the notebook going, in his own spelling.

volumes.title: A Rose on a Broken Wall
volumes.text:
July. I have taken the gatehouse at Brindle Hall, three miles up the Ember from Emberwick, on a seven-year lease and a great deal of optimism. The Hall itself lost its roof in a storm forty years ago. What the agent's letter called a rose garden is a square of brambles between fallen walls, with a sundial lying on its face.

I am Ottoline Brack, lately a teacher of arithmetic. I have grown roses in four pots on a windowsill. I mention this so that what follows is understood.

On my first evening I climbed the rubble to see what I had done. High on the broken east wall, out of reach, one rose was in flower: white, with a blush at the heart, and a scent of apples that carried down to me in the dusk. Nobody can tell me its name. I intend to find out.

volumes.title: Under the Brambles
volumes.text:
August. Three weeks of clearing brambles at Brindle Hall, and I have the scratches of a woman who keeps forty cats. I had a billhook, leather gauntlets and a bonfire that sulked. The brambles had forty years' start.

Under them, though, the rose garden is still there. I have uncovered stone edging round four long beds, a path of worn brick laid in herringbone, and the plinth where the sundial stood. I also found eleven rose stumps, dead as doornails, and one rusted label that crumbled as I picked it up.

The ruin part of the bargain is plain enough. The west wall leans. The south wall is a heap. Only the east wall stands to its full height, and the white rose rides along the top of it where nobody can prune it, feed it or spoil it. I am beginning to think that is how it survived.

volumes.title: What Mrs. Fenn Remembers
volumes.text:
September. Old Mrs. Fenn of Mill Lane was the daughter of the last head gardener at Brindle Hall, and she came up in the carrier's cart. She is eighty-three. She walked the brick path with a stick and named every dead stump from memory.

When I pointed to the white rose on the east wall she stood a long while. Her father, she said, raised a rose at the Hall called the Ember Maid, white with a blush, and it was never grown anywhere else. Everyone believes it went when the roof did. She would not say this was it until she could smell it in flower.

It is past flowering now. So I leaned a ladder on the wall, cut thirteen shoots, and set twelve in a trench of sandy soil behind the gatehouse. The thirteenth, an afterthought, went in a cracked pot by the pump.

volumes.title: The Duchess Pays a Call
volumes.text:
October. I write this in a temper. Mr. Dunmow, who farms the land beside Brindle Hall, keeps a white goat named Duchess. She has a beard, yellow eyes and no respect for a hurdle fence.

Yesterday I walked to Emberwick for lamp oil. When I came back, Duchess was standing in my cutting trench with the air of a guest who has enjoyed her dinner. Of the twelve cuttings from the white rose on the east wall, eleven were eaten to the ground. She was chewing the twelfth as I arrived, like someone tasting soup.

Mr. Dunmow came for her at dusk and promised a cartload of manure by way of apology. It is too late in the year to take more cuttings. All I have left is one thin afterthought in a cracked pot by the pump, which I do not expect to live.

volumes.title: Twelve Roses by Carrier
volumes.text:
November. The carrier from Emberwick brought a bundle of sticks wrapped in wet sacking, and with it most of my savings in another form. Twelve bare-root roses, ordered from a nursery in the Lowlands to fill the four old beds at Brindle Hall. I chose them from a catalogue by lamplight, which is how all foolish things are chosen.

There are three each of Widow Harrowby, a deep crimson; Marsh Lantern, yellow; Captain Thrale, striped pink and white like a boiled sweet; and Fellside Pearl, cream. So the catalogue says. At present they are twelve thorny twigs.

I planted them in driving rain with Mr. Dunmow's apology manure under each, spreading the roots like fingers on a table. His goat watched from behind a newly mended fence. The one cutting in the cracked pot by the pump has kept its two leaves, for what that is worth.

volumes.title: The East Wall Comes Down
volumes.text:
December. On the night of the fourteenth a gale came off the Northern Fells and blew till morning. Some time after three there was a long, low roar from the garden, like a cart of coals being tipped.

At first light I went out. The top third of the east wall at Brindle Hall had fallen into the nettles, and the white rose with it. Forty years it rode up there, out of everyone's reach. Now it lay under a ton of stone, with one snapped cane sticking up like a hand.

I am not ashamed to say I sat down on the sundial plinth and cried. Then I counted. The twelve new roses in the beds were untouched. The pot by the pump had blown over, but the cutting was still in it. I stood it up again. One does what one can reach.

volumes.title: The Head Gardener's Ledger
volumes.text:
January. The ground at Brindle Hall is iron, so I have been gardening at a table in Emberwick Library instead. They hold the Hall's garden ledgers there, forty years of them, in the hand of Mrs. Fenn's father. He wrote small and wasted nothing.

I found his rose in the eleventh ledger. Ember Maid, raised here from seed. White, blushed at the centre like a child come in from the cold. Scent of apples. Seven leaflets to the leaf, not five. Slow from cuttings: one in a dozen strikes, if the gardener is lucky and leaves it alone.

One in a dozen. I copied the page out twice. Then I walked the three miles home in the frost, went straight to the cracked pot by the pump, and counted the leaflets on my cutting's last leaf. Seven. It proves very little. I counted them again anyway.

volumes.title: A Lesson in Pruning
volumes.text:
February. Every book agrees that roses are pruned in late winter and disagrees about everything else. Cut hard, says one. Cut lightly, says another. A third has diagrams like a geometry problem, and I taught geometry, and I still could not follow it.

So I knelt in the four beds at Brindle Hall with new secateurs and did my best with the twelve young roses. Mr. Dunmow, passing with his goat on a rope, watched me take Captain Thrale down to the height of an egg cup. “Bit severe,” he said. He was right. I had cut two of the three below every bud.

That afternoon he and his boy barrowed the fallen stone of the east wall off the buried white rose. The old root is there, thick as my wrist, split but not torn out. Whether it lives is not for us to say.

volumes.title: Red Shoots
volumes.text:
March. Good news, and I hardly dare write it down in case it notices. At the foot of the broken east wall at Brindle Hall, the old white rose has put up three shoots from its split root. They are dark red, fat as asparagus, and have come through the rubble as though stone were a small matter.

And the cutting in the cracked pot by the pump, the afterthought, the only one the goat missed: I tipped it out today and found white roots circling the soil. One in a dozen, the old ledger said. It was one in thirteen, but I shall not quibble.

Ten of my twelve bought roses are in bud. The two Captain Thrales I pruned to nothing remain nothing. I have moved the cutting into the gatehouse porch and built a fence round the porch. Duchess has been seen looking at it.

volumes.title: Greenfly and a Late Frost
volumes.text:
April. I had not understood that everything on earth eats roses. This month it was greenfly, packed along every new shoot in the four beds like passengers on a market-day cart. I rubbed them off with finger and thumb for an hour each morning, and each morning they were back, with relations.

Then, on the twentieth, a frost. The tender tips of the Marsh Lanterns went brown and limp overnight. I walked round the garden at Brindle Hall saying words I never used in a schoolroom.

Mrs. Fenn sent advice by the carrier: leave the greenfly and wait for the ladybirds. Within the week they came, red and spotted, and the blue tits with them, and the shoots were clean. The frosted tips have broken again lower down. The three red shoots on the old wall rose are knee high. I measure them daily, which helps nobody.

volumes.title: Buds in the Rain
volumes.text:
May. Rain every day for a fortnight, and the garden at Brindle Hall has gone soft and green and slightly mouldy, like a cheese. There is mildew on the Widow Harrowby and black spots on the leaves of Fellside Pearl. The sundial is upright on its plinth again, though it has had no sun to tell.

But there are buds. I have counted sixty-one on the ten bought roses, tight and green, each with a thread of colour at the tip.

On the old white rose by the east wall, one of the three new shoots carries a cluster of five. Whether they will open white and smell of apples, I cannot know for three weeks. I have asked Mrs. Fenn of Mill Lane to come at midsummer. She replied on a postcard: I have waited forty years. I can manage three weeks.

volumes.title: The Ember Maid
volumes.text:
June. Midsummer Eve at Brindle Hall. Half the garden is still a ruin: the west wall leans, the south wall is a heap of stone, and two Captain Thrales never came back from my pruning. But ten roses are in flower in the four old beds, crimson, yellow and cream.

Mrs. Fenn came up in the carrier's cart at four. She went straight past all of it to the foot of the east wall, where the old rose had opened three of its five buds that morning. White, blushed at the heart. She bent, with my arm to steady her, and breathed in. “Apples,” she said. “That's my father's rose.” Then she asked for a chair.

So the Ember Maid is not lost. There are two of her now, counting the cutting in the porch. Duchess the goat looked on over the fence. She was not invited.

volumes.title: The Wager
volumes.text:
January. I am Mrs. Dab, cook at the Copper Kettle inn on Emberwick market square, and I have made a wager I may regret. At last month's Midwinter Supper the sprouts came from the greengrocer and tasted of the cart. I said so. Mr. Ost, the landlord, said I was welcome to do better.

So it is agreed, in writing. Next Midwinter I am to feed forty guests with every vegetable and fruit on the table grown in the kitchen plot behind the inn. If I manage it, he buys me a new copper preserving pan. If I fail, I never mention the greengrocer again.

The plot is twenty paces by twelve and mostly dock. The gardener, Tob Wren, is seventy-one and speaks about twice a day. He looked at the paper, then at the plot. “Parsnips,” he said. I take that as a yes.

volumes.title: Beans and Buckets
volumes.text:
February. The kitchen plot behind the Copper Kettle is dug, and Tob Wren did most of the digging at the speed of a man winding a clock. I carried away dock roots in a coal scuttle. If I am to win my wager with Mr. Ost and serve the Midwinter Supper from this ground, I had better know what is in it.

Today we sowed broad beans, two rows, each bean pushed in to the depth of a thumb. Seed potatoes are sitting in egg trays on my pantry windowsill, growing stubby purple shoots. Tob calls this chitting. He has put an upturned bucket over the old rhubarb crown to draw it up pale and early.

I asked what else I could do. He said, “Wait.” A cook is used to things being ready in forty minutes. This is going to be a long year.

volumes.title: Parsnips Teach Patience
volumes.text:
March. We sowed the parsnips today, the first crop meant for the Midwinter table itself. Nine months in the ground, Tob Wren says, and three weeks before they so much as show. The seed is like flakes of brown paper and blows away if you breathe. I sowed one row and lost half of it to a gust across the Copper Kettle's yard.

Onion sets went in too, two hundred of them, each pressed into the soil with its tip just showing. By next morning the blackbirds had pulled out thirty and left them lying on the path. I pushed them back. They pulled them out again.

Mr. Ost strolled down the plot with his hands behind him and asked whether I had ordered from the greengrocer yet, just in case. I said the only thing I required from him was the price of a preserving pan.

volumes.title: The Landlord's Old Coat
volumes.text:
April. War in the kitchen plot. The peas came up in a neat green line on Monday, and by Wednesday the pigeons from the Copper Kettle's stable roof had eaten a third of them. On Thursday night the slugs took the first carrots and left a silver signature.

Tob Wren and I have answered. He stretched black thread on sticks over the peas. I go out after dark with a lantern and a jam jar, collecting slugs, and what the kitchen maids think of their cook I do not ask. We resowed the carrots and ringed the row with ashes from my range.

We have also put up a scarecrow. It wears a coat Mr. Ost threw out and a pudding basin for a hat. From the taproom window the likeness is remarkable. Two customers have greeted it. The pigeons are less convinced, but the thread holds.

volumes.title: Paper Hats for Beans
volumes.text:
May. The kitchen plot is filling. Potatoes are earthed up in ridges, onions stand like green quills, and today Tob Wren and I planted out the leeks. You make a hole with a dibber, drop the seedling in, fill the hole with water and walk away. It looks like neglect. Tob says it is the proper way, and Tob has been right about everything since February, which is wearing.

We sowed the winter crops too, in a seedbed by the wall: sprouts, red cabbage and kale. These are for my wager, the Midwinter Supper for forty.

On the twelfth the sky cleared at dusk and Tob sniffed the air. “Frost,” he said. We covered every runner bean with a cone of newspaper from the Copper Kettle's taproom, forty-six paper hats in two rows. By morning the grass was white. The beans had not noticed.

volumes.title: What a Cook May Eat
volumes.text:
June. The first new potatoes came out of the kitchen plot today, pale as eggs, and I boiled them with mint within the half hour. Tob Wren ate nine. Mr. Ost, the landlord, ate eleven and said they were tolerable, which from him is poetry.

Here is my difficulty. Everything in this plot wants eating now, and my wager is about December. If I serve the Copper Kettle's guests every pea and carrot as it ripens, there will be nothing for the Midwinter Supper but good intentions.

So Tob has run a length of twine down the middle of the plot. East of it is the summer kitchen: peas, lettuces, early potatoes, broad beans. West of it is the store ground: maincrop potatoes, onions, parsnips, leeks, carrots, the winter greens. Nobody picks west of the twine. I have told the kitchen maids. I have also, with more effort, told myself.

volumes.title: Forty Jars
volumes.text:
July. The kitchen at the Copper Kettle smells of vinegar, and my hands are stained the colour of a brown boot. The plot has given more than forty guests could eat in a month, all in the same fortnight, so I am putting summer into jars against the Midwinter Supper.

So far: twelve jars of pickled shallots, nine of beetroot, eight of runner beans laid down in salt, six of blackcurrant jam, and five of a green tomato relish I invented in a panic. Forty jars. One for each guest, Tob Wren pointed out, which is the longest remark he has made since spring.

I am doing all this in the old preserving pan, the one with the dent and the loose handle. It boiled over twice. I mentioned this to Mr. Ost. He said a pan was a pan, and December a long way off.

volumes.title: Onions on a String
volumes.text:
August. The onions have fallen over, which alarmed me until Tob Wren explained that it is what onions do when they are finished. We lifted them and laid them on the path behind the Copper Kettle to dry in the sun, like a street paved in gold cobbles. Tob showed me how to plait them onto string. Mine look like a child's first knitting, but they hold.

The winter cabbages are another matter. The white butterflies found them, and now every leaf carries a crew of green caterpillars eating my wager.

There is no clever cure. Tob and I pick them off by hand each evening and drop them over the wall for the hens next door, who think very well of us. I counted two hundred and six in one night. Mr. Ost watched from the back door and asked if this was what I called cooking.

volumes.title: Six Sacks and a Scare
volumes.text:
September. We lifted the maincrop potatoes this week, Tob Wren forking and I picking up behind him. On the second row the leaves were blotched brown and the first potatoes came up soft and foul. Blight. Tob cut the tops off every row and burned them at the far end of the plot.

I did not sleep well. A Midwinter Supper for forty without potatoes is a wager lost.

But we lost only that one row. The rest came up clean and dry, and we filled six sacks, which now stand in the dark of the Copper Kettle's cellar with their necks tied. The old apple tree by the wall gave four baskets as well. I wrapped each sound apple in a twist of paper and laid them in trays, not touching. Mr. Ost came down to count the sacks. He counted twice and went away quiet.

volumes.title: A Cat for the Cellar
volumes.text:
October. Tob Wren and I lifted the carrots and packed them in boxes of dry sand in the Copper Kettle's cellar, like putting children to bed. Nine squashes sit on the shelf above my range, hardening their skins. The onions hang in ropes from the scullery beam and knock the kitchen maids' caps off.

I found a carrot box dug into and two apples gnawed. Mice. I will not be beaten at Midwinter by something that weighs less than an egg.

So the inn's cat, Mrs. Biggins, has been promoted. She is large, grey and not ambitious, but she now sleeps on the potato sacks with a saucer of milk for wages, and nothing has been touched since. I also caught Mr. Ost in the cellar with a candle, lifting lids. He claimed to be looking for a barrel. The barrels are on the other side.

volumes.title: Frost on the Parsnips
volumes.text:
November. First hard frost on the kitchen plot, and Tob Wren was pleased for once. Frost turns a parsnip sweet, he says. We have left them in the ground since March, and I dug one to try. It was as long as my forearm. Roasted, it tasted of honey and chestnuts. I ate it alone at the kitchen table and told nobody.

West of the twine the winter ground stands ready: forty-two leeks thick as broom handles, a row of sprouts like knobbly walking sticks, eleven red cabbages hard as cannonballs, kale past counting.

I have drafted the bill of fare for the Midwinter Supper three times. I counted the leeks, then the potatoes sack by sack, then the jars. On paper there is enough. A cook does not trust paper. Mr. Ost of the Copper Kettle asked today what size a preserving pan usually is.

volumes.title: The Midwinter Supper
volumes.text:
December. It is done, and I write this at midnight with my feet in a basin of hot water. Forty guests sat down at the Copper Kettle to the Midwinter Supper, and every vegetable and fruit before them came from the plot behind the inn.

Leek and potato soup. Parsnips roasted in dripping, carrots glazed, red cabbage stewed with apple, sprouts in browned butter, squash baked whole. Pickled shallots and beetroot down the middle of each table. Apple pudding, and blackcurrant jam with the cheese. Tob Wren sat by the fire and had first helping of everything. He said, “Good parsnips.”

Mr. Ost stood up at the end and paid his wager: a copper preserving pan, wide as a cartwheel, with my name stamped on the handle. I have hung it where he must pass it daily. A seed list came in this morning's post.
